heading: Energy Substrates and Bioenergetic Fatigue
bullets: Energy substrates provide the essential starting materials for biological energy pathways
Key substrates include phosphagens (ATP and CP), glucose, glycogen, lactate, free fatty acids, and amino acids
Physical fatigue during exercise is predominantly linked to the depletion of phosphagens and glycogen
Substrates like free fatty acids, lactate, and amino acids rarely deplete to performance-limiting levels
Depletion and repletion kinetics of phosphagens and glycogen dictate exercise capacity and recovery
transcript: Welcome, class. Today we are examining Section 3.3: Substrate Depletion and Repletion. When an athlete exercises, whether they are performing a maximal clean and jerk or running a marathon, their performance is fundamentally constrained by the availability of energy substrates. In bioenergetics, substrates are defined as the starting molecules that fuel metabolic pathways. These include phosphagens—specifically adenosine triphosphate and creatine phosphate—as well as glucose, glycogen, lactate, free fatty acids, and amino acids. Now, a critical physiological concept here is selective depletion. As exercise intensity and duration vary, certain substrates are drained rapidly while others remain largely intact. In sports science, muscular fatigue is primarily and directly linked to the exhaustion of phosphagens and glycogen. Substrates such as free fatty acids, lactate, and amino acids do not typically decline to the point where they limit exercise capacity. Therefore, understanding the exact depletion and repletion patterns of phosphagens and carbohydrates forms the scientific cornerstone for designing training sessions, interset rest intervals, and post-workout nutritional strategies.

heading: Intramuscular Phosphagen Depletion Dynamics
bullets: High-intensity anaerobic exertion depletes muscle phosphagens substantially faster than aerobic exercise
Creatine phosphate decreases 50% to 70% during the initial 5 to 30 seconds of high-intensity exercise
Intense exercise to exhaustion can result in almost complete depletion of intramuscular creatine phosphate
Muscle ATP declines by up to 50% to 60% during induced fatigue, protected by CP hydrolysis and myokinase
Dynamic muscle actions producing external work consume more metabolic energy and deplete phosphagens more than isometric actions
transcript: Let's begin by breaking down phosphagen depletion. When an athlete performs short-term, explosive anaerobic work, intramuscular phosphagen stores are drawn down at a staggering rate compared to steady-state aerobic exercise. Creatine phosphate, or CP, serves as our immediate high-energy buffer. During the first stage of high-intensity exercise—lasting just 5 to 30 seconds—muscle CP concentrations drop by 50 to 70 percent. If the athlete continues exercising intensely to exhaustion, CP stores can be virtually depleted. In contrast, intramuscular ATP concentrations are defended far more aggressively. ATP levels may drop only slightly or decline by up to 50 to 60 percent during severe fatigue. Why doesn't ATP drop to zero? Because cell survival depends on it, and the rapid breakdown of creatine phosphate, alongside the myokinase reaction and early glycogenolysis, continuously regenerates ATP to sustain crossbridge cycling. Furthermore, research demonstrates that dynamic muscle actions that produce external work consume significantly more metabolic energy and deplete phosphagens to a greater degree than static isometric contractions.

heading: Phosphagen Repletion Kinetics and Recovery Pathways
bullets: Post-exercise phosphagen replenishment occurs rapidly across a distinct biphasic recovery timeline
Complete resynthesis of intramuscular ATP occurs within 3 to 5 minutes following cessation of exercise
Complete resynthesis of creatine phosphate (CP) requires approximately 8 minutes of recovery
Phosphagen repletion is primarily fueled by aerobic metabolism through mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation
Glycolytic flux can also contribute to post-exercise recovery following high-intensity bouts
transcript: Now that we understand how fast phosphagens drain, let's examine their repletion kinetics. Fortunately for strength and conditioning coaches, phosphagen resynthesis is remarkably rapid. Complete resynthesis of intramuscular ATP occurs within approximately 3 to 5 minutes following exercise. Meanwhile, the complete rephosphorylation of creatine back into creatine phosphate takes about 8 minutes. Notice how this biological timeline directly informs the interset rest periods prescribed in heavy resistance training and plyometrics. If you want an athlete to express true maximal power in a subsequent set, they require adequate recovery time for phosphagens to rebuild. Mechanistically, phosphagen repletion is an aerobic process: mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation provides the ATP necessary to rephosphorylate creatine in the sarcoplasm. However, research also indicates that anaerobic glycolysis can contribute to recovery following high-intensity exercise. Understanding these timeframes allows coaches to manipulate work-to-rest ratios to target specific energy systems.

heading: Training Adaptations in Phosphagen Storage
bullets: Aerobic endurance training can increase resting phosphagen levels and reduce depletion rates at absolute workloads
Depletion rates at relative submaximal power outputs (percent of VO2max) remain unchanged with aerobic training
Short-term sprint training (8 weeks) and explosive training (6 months) generally do not alter baseline phosphagen concentrations
Sprint training increases total phosphagen content primarily through muscular hypertrophy
Five weeks of resistance training increased triceps brachii resting phosphagen concentration via Type II fiber hypertrophy
transcript: How does chronic exercise training alter our phosphagen reserves? The adaptations are nuanced and depend heavily on training modality. Aerobic endurance training has been shown to elevate resting phosphagen concentrations and reduce the rate of phosphagen depletion when working at a given absolute submaximal power output—though when measured at the same relative percentage of maximal capacity, depletion rates remain similar. With anaerobic sprint and explosive training, short-term studies spanning eight weeks of sprinting or six months of resistance exercise generally show no major changes in resting phosphagen concentration per unit of muscle. However, total intramuscular phosphagen content in the body often increases simply because the athlete gains muscle mass. Interestingly, one notable study demonstrated that five weeks of targeted resistance training significantly increased resting phosphagen concentrations in the triceps brachii. Researchers hypothesize this occurs because resistance training induces selective hypertrophy of fast-twitch Type II fibers, which naturally possess higher baseline concentrations of phosphagens than Type I fibers.

heading: Glycogen Storage Capacity and Tissue Distribution
bullets: Intramuscular glycogen stores total approximately 300 to 400 g across the body's entire skeletal musculature
The human liver stores roughly 70 to 100 g of glycogen to maintain systemic blood glucose homeostasis
Baseline resting glycogen concentrations are highly responsive to both training status and dietary manipulation
Anaerobic conditioning (sprinting and lifting) and aerobic endurance training both elevate resting muscle glycogen
Elevations in resting muscle glycogen stores require appropriate, concomitant post-exercise carbohydrate nutrition
transcript: Moving from the phosphagens to our primary carbohydrate fuel, let's explore glycogen distribution and storage limits. Unlike adipose tissue, which provides a virtually limitless reservoir of fatty acids, human glycogen stores are strictly finite. The entire skeletal muscle mass of an average adult stores approximately 300 to 400 grams of glycogen, while the liver stores between 70 and 100 grams. Intramuscular glycogen is held locally for muscular contraction, whereas hepatic glycogen serves as a systemic glucose reservoir to defend circulating blood glucose levels. Resting concentrations of both liver and muscle glycogen are exceptionally dynamic. Through proper training adaptations and dietary manipulations, these stores can be significantly augmented. Specifically, research demonstrates that both anaerobic training—such as sprinting and resistance exercise—and traditional aerobic endurance training elevate baseline muscle glycogen stores, provided the athlete consumes appropriate carbohydrate nutrition during post-exercise recovery.

heading: Exercise Intensity and Muscle Glycogenolysis Rates
bullets: The rate of muscle glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) is directly determined by exercise intensity
Increases in relative intensity of 50%, 75%, and 100% of VO2max increase glycogenolysis to 0.7, 1.4, and 3.4 mmol/kg/min
Muscle glycogen serves as the predominant carbohydrate fuel during moderate- to high-intensity exercise
At exercise intensities exceeding 60% of VO2max, muscle glycogen becomes an increasingly critical energy substrate
During strenuous exercise above 60% of VO2max, the entire glycogen store of specific active muscle cells can be depleted
transcript: Now let's examine how exercise intensity governs carbohydrate utilization. The rate of muscle glycogenolysis—the enzymatic breakdown of stored glycogen into glucose units—is directly proportional to the intensity of muscular work. As exercise intensity climbs from 50 percent, to 75 percent, to 100 percent of maximal oxygen uptake, the rate of muscle glycogenolysis accelerates from 0.7, to 1.4, up to 3.4 millimoles per kilogram of muscle per minute. That is nearly a five-fold acceleration in carbohydrate breakdown. Muscle glycogen is far more important than liver glycogen during moderate- and high-intensity efforts. In fact, once exercise intensity rises above 60 percent of VO2 max, muscle glycogen becomes an indispensable substrate. At these higher workloads, metabolic flux is so intense that the entire glycogen content of specific, recruited muscle fibers can become completely exhausted during the training bout.

heading: Endurance Duration, Liver Glycogen, and Hypoglycemia
bullets: Liver glycogen contribution increases progressively with exercise duration to support blood glucose
At intensities below 50% VO2max, low muscle uptake maintains stable blood glucose; levels fall slightly beyond 90 minutes
Prolonged exercise exceeding 90 minutes above 50% VO2max can severely deplete liver glycogen stores
A decline in circulating blood glucose to 2.5–3.0 mmol/L reduces carbohydrate oxidation and triggers exhaustion
Clinical hypoglycemic reactions may occur in susceptible individuals when blood glucose drops below 2.5 mmol/L
transcript: What happens when exercise duration extends over prolonged periods? That brings us to liver glycogen dynamics and blood glucose maintenance. At low exercise intensities below 50 percent of VO2 max, muscle glucose uptake is minimal, and blood glucose concentrations remain remarkably stable. However, as activity extends beyond 90 minutes, even at low intensities, blood glucose gradually drifts downward, though rarely below 2.8 millimoles per liter. In contrast, during long-term exercise exceeding 90 minutes at intensities above 50 percent of VO2 max, the working muscles take up substantial circulating glucose. To maintain homeostasis, the liver continually breaks down its glycogen reserves. Once hepatic glycogen becomes severely depleted, blood glucose drops to around 2.5 to 3.0 millimoles per liter. This precipitous fall impairs cellular carbohydrate oxidation and induces profound physical exhaustion—what endurance athletes refer to as 'hitting the wall.' Furthermore, when blood glucose drops below 2.5 millimoles per liter, individuals may suffer severe hypoglycemic reactions.

heading: Glycogen Depletion Dynamics in Resistance Training
bullets: High-intensity intermittent resistance exercise causes substantial muscle glycogen depletion of 20% to 60%
Marked glycogen reductions occur with relatively few resistance training sets and low total workloads
Phosphagens limit high-resistance, low-repetition bouts; glycogen limits multi-set, high-work-volume sessions
Resistance exercise induces selective glycogen depletion, preferentially exhausting fast-twitch Type II fibers
When total mechanical work is equal, the absolute magnitude of glycogen depletion is identical regardless of intensity
transcript: Many students mistakenly assume that glycogen depletion only occurs during endurance marathons, but Section 3.3 highlights a critical finding: resistance training also heavily drains muscle glycogen. High-intensity, intermittent resistance exercise can reduce muscle glycogen stores by 20 to 60 percent across relatively few sets. Now, consider the bioenergetic limiting factor: during very heavy resistance exercise involving few repetitions and low set volume, phosphagen availability is the primary limiting factor. However, when an athlete performs bodybuilding or hypertrophy protocols featuring numerous total sets and high mechanical workloads, muscle glycogen becomes the performance-limiting constraint. Furthermore, resistance exercise causes selective glycogen depletion, predominantly draining fast-twitch Type II fibers. Finally, remember this key biomechanical rule from the literature: while higher intensity increases the instantaneous rate of glycogenolysis, when total external work performed is held equal, the absolute amount of muscle glycogen depleted is the same, regardless of training intensity.

heading: Muscle Glycogen Repletion and Nutrition Protocols
bullets: Muscle glycogen replenishment following exercise is strictly dependent on post-workout carbohydrate ingestion
Optimal repletion occurs when ingesting 0.7 to 3.0 g of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight every 2 hours
Carbohydrate feeding maximizes resynthesis at 5 to 6 mmol/g wet muscle per hour during the first 4 to 6 hours
Complete muscle glycogen replenishment occurs within 24 hours under adequate carbohydrate intake conditions
High eccentric exercise causing muscle damage significantly prolongs the timeline required for complete glycogen repletion
transcript: We conclude Section 3.3 with the science of post-exercise glycogen resynthesis. Rebuilding depleted muscle glycogen is heavily dictated by nutritional timing and carbohydrate intake. Research indicates that glycogen repletion is optimized when an athlete consumes 0.7 to 3.0 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight every two hours post-exercise. This dietary strategy drives glycogen resynthesis rates of 5 to 6 millimoles per gram of wet muscle per hour during the critical four-to-six-hour recovery window. Under optimal nutritional conditions, complete muscle glycogen stores can be fully replenished within 24 hours. However, strength coaches and clinicians must heed an essential caveat: if the preceding exercise included a substantial eccentric component—which induces microtrauma and structural muscle damage—glycogen resynthesis is substantially impaired, and the athlete will require more time to fully restore their muscle carbohydrate reserves. Thank you, class, and I will see you in our next lecture on Section 3.4!
